newsitem.title: UK: British Midland may buy quick-change B737s.
newsitem.headline: British Midland may buy quick-change B737s.

text.p: British Midland is considering acquiring Boeing 737QCs (quick-change) for use as passenger aircraft during the day and freighters overnight, cargo manager Terry Greetham said.

"Lufthansa, with support from DHL, has shown with its 'Flash' express product that 737s in QC configuration can be successfully used and I can see a night application for this aircraft with British Midland," he told Reuters.
He added that the airline already used its standard passenger 737-300s to operate a nightly return service between London Heathrow and Edinburgh on behalf of Royal Mail.
"This operation has demonstrated what we can achieve overnight," he said.

The Royal Mail 'Nightjet' operation involves carrying up to 13 tonnes of mailbags and parcels on covered seats but the aircraft used does not have the additional capacity or flexibility provided by the QC version of the plane.

"While we (the cargo division) are quite happy to live in the shadow of British Midland's main business priority -- carrying business class passengers -- my job is nevertheless to maximise revenues earned by the cargo by-product," said Greetham.

"I see one of the ways of doing this as using convertible aircraft in a night freighter role," he added, although he said he had not yet made a firm recommendation to the British Midland board for the purchase of 737QCs.

"It (the purchase) may or may not occur but it would lead to better utilisation of our aircraft. If it can be proven that the versatility of our fleet will be improved by getting QCs then we will do it," he said.
Greetham identified routes linking London Heathrow, Paris, Brussels, Amsterdam and Cologne as being ideal for an overnight British Midland cargo operation.
"We would expect to attract customers such as Royal Mail for these services," he stated.
British Midland currently operates 42 short- and medium-haul aircraft, a fleet that comprises mainly Boeing 737s (-500s, -400s and -300s) supported by Fokker F100s.
In early April, the carrier announced a $1 billion order for eight A321 and 12 A320 aircraft from Airbus Industrie.

"We are keen to see what impact the arrival of the Airbus will have on our cargo operations. While the cargo capacity will be double that we can carry on our 737s, larger aircraft will mean reduced frequencies," said Greetham.
"But on the other hand, that will give us better utilisation of airport slots, which will mean we can add more destinations over the next two years," he added.
